headline: UK medical cannabis: clinicians split on psychiatry evidence
dek: At a London symposium on 26 November, a King's College psychiatrist called UK prescribing backwards; David Nutt and Mike Barnes backed registry data.
key_points: King's College London's Edward Chesney said the UK legalised prescribing before running trials, and that daily doses of a gram or more of flower are not evidence-based.
Drug Science's Michael Lynskey said a recent meta-analysis found little trial evidence in mental health, but observational registries show benefit with mostly mild side effects.
Prof. Mike Barnes cited UK registry data on about 100 autistic patients and 68 ADHD patients showing gains in anxiety, sleep and quality of life, and called cannabis a reasonable second-line option.
Speakers backed practical fixes: collateral history from family, linking private prescribing data with national records, and better patient education.
body: Britain's private medical cannabis sector is still arguing about what counts as evidence. At the Cannabis Health Symposium in London on 26 November, the afternoon sessions set clinicians who want randomised controlled trials against researchers who say patient registries already show enough benefit to justify prescribing, according to a detailed account published by Business of Cannabis on 27 November.

The split matters most in psychiatry, where many UK patients are prescribed unlicensed cannabis flower for anxiety, depression, sleep and ADHD. As we reported on 26 November, the morning sessions heard that 2.34 million items were dispensed in a single year. The afternoon turned to whether that prescribing rests on firm ground.
## The case against prescribing first

Edward Chesney, a clinical lecturer at King's College London, said the UK had approached the question backwards by allowing prescribing before trials were run. He placed cannabis closer to opioids or benzodiazepines in its risk profile and described himself as a committed believer in clinical trials. On psychosis, he pointed to a probable causal link, especially with high-potency products, citing a recent Mendelian randomisation study and a series of 17 cases at the Maudsley hospital.

Chesney was blunt on dose. Most trials used about 15mg of oral THC, he said, while he sees patients at a Brixton addiction service who are prescribed a gram or more of flower a day. A daily dose of 40mg of THC, he said, is not evidence-based. He also conceded a gap in his own field: his PhD study recruited 30 people, 27 of them men.
## The case for real-world data

Professor Michael Lynskey of Drug Science, the independent scientific charity, accepted that a recent meta-analysis found little randomised trial evidence in mental health and none for depression. But he said observational registries, including his own, show benefit, with side effects mostly mild to moderate. He argued that recreational psychosis risk is probably overestimated and is strongest in people who start before 15, while medical patients average around 40 years old.

James Smith, chief revenue officer and co-founder of 4C Labs, went further, saying cannabis does not cause psychosis. He cited testing of 550 seized products in which more than 48% were not cannabis or were adulterated. He said 4C Labs runs focus groups in Canada and EEG tests on each product, which he described as short of formal science but better than nothing.

In a separate session, Professor David Nutt of Imperial College London argued that randomised trials are the wrong yardstick and poor value, and that Bayesian methods could draw up to ten times more from the same data. He criticised NICE, the body that advises the NHS on treatments, for ignoring patient-reported outcomes. Nutt set up Project Twenty21, which Business of Cannabis described as the UK's largest medical cannabis registry, after the government did not fund research promised in 2018. He said there had been barely ten NHS prescriptions in eight years.
> The UK has a registry evidence base and a trial evidence base that do not agree. Regulators will eventually have to choose which one sets the rules.
## Autism and ADHD: second line, not first

Professor Mike Barnes, chair of the Medical Cannabis Clinicians Society, said autism affects about 0.6% of the population, roughly 400,000 people in the UK, and that about 30% do not respond to standard treatment, leaving an estimated 100,000 with significant unmet need. He cited a UK Medical Cannabis Registry study of about 100 autistic people showing significant improvements in anxiety, sleep and quality of life, but not in core autistic traits. Across about 10 studies covering about 400 patients, mostly children, he cited improvements of around 68% in anxiety and 75% in sleep and quality of life.

On ADHD, which he put at about 8% of children and 2% to 3% of adults, Barnes cited a registry case series of 68 patients with improvements at one, three and six months, some sustained to 12 months, and said about a third stopped another medication. His conclusion was measured: cannabis is not a first-line treatment for either condition, but it is a reasonable second, third or fourth-line option.
## A death that hangs over the debate

The psychiatry panel discussed Oliver Robinson, who died in November 2023 while prescribed medical cannabis for depression. Moderator Dr Michelle Nyangereka said a coroner found this year that the prescription contributed to his death; the clinic disputed parts of the finding. Chesney called for clinics to take collateral history, meaning input from a family member or friend who can flag concerns, and for private prescribing databases to be linked with national health records. Lynskey pointed to poor coordination between private psychiatry, GPs and clinics.

A patient panel added practical demands: short educational videos from clinics, supervised patient groups to replace informal Facebook and Discord forums, and fairer access. Patient advocate Nicola Stevenson said Network Rail applies a blanket ban on prescribed cannabis across its workforce. Julie Durrans, a prescribed patient, said she can afford her medicine only by cutting back elsewhere.
## What it means for operators

For UK clinics and suppliers, the direction of travel is towards more scrutiny of psychiatric prescribing, higher-dose flower and how patients are followed up. Proposals such as collateral history and data linkage would add cost and process, but they are the kind of safeguards that could head off tighter rules from regulators.
## What to watch

The overdue review by the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs is the main policy event ahead. Watch also for whether clinics adopt collateral-history checks voluntarily, whether registry groups publish more condition-specific outcomes, and whether any NHS trust moves beyond the handful of NHS prescriptions Nutt described.
